<a id="audit-mep-openings"></a>

### Audit MEP openings

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which of the openings already cut are now wrong.

Audits the openings already in the model against the MEP that is in it now. Answers the question a revision actually asks - *"the ducts moved, which of my openings are wrong?"* - with a status per opening: STALE (nothing runs through it any more), COMBINED (more than one service through one hole), UNHOSTED (not inside anything), or OK. Read-only. **THE TWO KINDS OF "OPENING" ARE NOT THE SAME KIND OF ELEMENT, AND THAT IS THE TRAP THIS FRAGMENT IS BUILT AROUND.** A cut void is a Revit `Opening`, which has NO SOLID at all - only a boundary and a host. A placed sleeve is a family instance, which does. The obvious way to gather openings returns mostly the first kind, so an audit written for the second reports "no geometry" for every one of them: no crash, no error, and an audit that audited nothing. Both kinds are handled, and each row SAYS WHICH ROUTE was used. **AN OPENING'S EXTENT IS TAKEN FROM ITS BOUNDARY AND ITS BOUNDING BOX, AND THE TWO ARE CROSS-CHECKED.** Where they disagree badly the row reads SUSPECT rather than being audited on geometry that may be in the wrong place. The documentation for the boundary does not state its coordinate space, so it is verified rather than assumed. **IT IS NOT CHECK_SLEEVE_SIZE.** That asks whether a hole is the right SIZE for what goes through it. This asks whether the hole is still in the right PLACE and still needed at all - the two questions a revision separates, and the reason creation and checking are different jobs. **STRUCTURE IN A LINK IS NOT SCANNED UNLESS ASKED FOR**, so without `includeLinks` the hosting question is answered against the host model only and says so. On a normal coordination job the walls and slabs are a link, which means a clean UNHOSTED count there has checked nothing. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, each opening's centre is looked for inside the walls, floors, roofs, ceilings and structural members of every loaded link, in each placement's own coordinates, and `linkedMatches` names what it sits in - the link, the type, the element's id IN THE LINK and its **Fire Rating**, which is what a penetration through the architect's wall actually has to answer. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". "Sits inside" is a box test, so a hole near a corner can name both walls - every candidate is listed. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `stale`, `combined` and `unhosted` stay this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-category-mismatch"></a>

### Check category mismatch

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** these are modelled in the wrong category.

Finds elements that ARE one thing but were MODELLED as another: the family or type name says louvre, damper or fan, and the element sits in a category that does not match. Hands the mismatches on as the set to look at, and changes nothing. **A WRONG CATEGORY IS INVISIBLE UNTIL IT MATTERS, AND THEN IT IS EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.** The element looks right on screen. It is the schedule that misses it, the view filter that does not catch it, the export that files it under the wrong discipline, and the clash test that ignores it. By the time one of those is noticed the model has been built on for weeks. **IT IS FOUND BY NAME BECAUSE THAT IS WHAT CARRIES THE INTENT.** Somebody named the family for what it is; the category is what they picked from a list, sometimes wrongly, sometimes because the right one was not available when the family was made. So the keywords are the caller's - the words this office uses for the thing - and no list is built in, because every job names its kit differently. **IT REPORTS WHERE THEY ACTUALLY ARE.** Knowing that eleven elements are in the wrong category is half an answer; knowing that seven are in generic models and four in casework says whether it was one mistake or several. **IT DOES NOT RE-CATEGORISE ANYTHING.** Changing a family's category is done in the family editor and it reloads through every instance in the project - it is a real piece of work with real consequences, not a repair to slip into a check. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is walked the same way and `linkedMatches` gives each link's line: how many are named like the thing but in the wrong category, where they actually are, and how many were right - a door built as a generic model in the architect's link breaks a door schedule as surely as one here. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements`, `foundIn` and the two counts stay this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-ceiling-coordination"></a>

### Check ceiling coordination

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** are the ceiling devices actually sitting in the ceiling.

Checks ceiling-mounted devices against the ceiling they are supposed to be in - is there a ceiling above each one at all, and is the device sitting AT it or floating above or hanging below. The sweep before a reflected ceiling plan is issued. Read-only. **THE FAULT THIS CATCHES IS INVISIBLE IN PLAN.** A diffuser 40 mm above the ceiling and a diffuser exactly in it look identical from above and both look fine in the browser. It shows up as a site query, or on a section nobody cut. Every device's own height is compared against the ceiling actually over it and the difference is reported in millimetres. **BEFORE THIS, THE QUESTION RESOLVED TO `SNAP_TO_GRID` - which MOVES things.** A question about whether the model is right, answered by something that changes it. **THE CEILING IS FOUND BY CASTING A RAY UPWARD, and that is the technique that works.** A device placed unhosted is not "hosted by" the ceiling in any readable way, and a room cannot tell you its own ceiling. The ray needs a real 3D view; if the project has none, that is REPORTED rather than returned as zero findings. **"NO CEILING ABOVE" IS A FINDING, NOT AN ERROR.** A device in an open-soffit area is fine; a device that should be in a ceiling and has none is either in the wrong place or the ceiling is missing from the model. Counted separately, because those two cases look identical in every other check. **THE RAY GOES UP FROM THE INSERTION POINT**, and for a family whose insertion point is off its own centre - some linear diffusers, some light fittings - it can miss the ceiling beside it. A large NO CEILING count in an area known to have one is usually that, and the report says so rather than letting it read as a hundred real faults. **CEILINGS IN LINKS ARE NOT HIT UNLESS ASKED FOR.** Architecture is normally linked, so a host model with no ceilings reports everything as uncovered - said on the summary line, because it looks exactly like a real finding. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, a second ray is cast with Revit's own FindReferencesInRevitLinks, and every device whose nearest ceiling above is a LINKED one gets a line in `linkedMatches`: the gap, the verdict against the same tolerance, and the ceiling's type and id IN THE LINK - on an MEP model the ceilings are the architect's, so this is the answer the host-only run warns it cannot give. **The ray sees a link only where the 3D view shows it**, and the answer names that view. `linksSearched` says how many links are loaded: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `outOfPlane` and `noCeilingAbove` stay this model's answer (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-datums-against-link"></a>

### Check datums against link

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-20 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** whether this model's grids and levels sit where the same grids and levels sit in one linked model, within a tolerance.

Checks this model's grids and levels against the grids and levels of one linked model - the architect's or the structural link - and says for each datum whether it is aligned within the tolerance, off and by how much in millimetres and degrees, not checked and why, or only in one of the two models. Grids and levels are matched by name, and a link datum whose name is not found here is matched to one here that lines up, flagged as a name that differs. Counts the datums that are off and hands on their ids to select. It changes nothing.

<a id="check-equipment-clearance"></a>

### Check equipment clearance

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** is the maintenance space round this equipment clear.

Checks the maintenance and access zone around each piece of equipment - the space in front for pulling a coil or opening a panel door, at the sides, above for the valves - and reports everything modelled inside it. *"Can this be serviced once the building is up"*, answered from the model instead of on site. Read-only. **THE ZONE IS DIRECTIONAL, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT.** A plain *"keep a metre clear all round"* is not how equipment is serviced: an air handling unit needs a metre and a half in FRONT for coil withdrawal and 200 mm behind. A check that cannot tell those apart either passes real obstructions or fails on the wall the unit is meant to stand against - and both make it useless. Each face carries its own figure. **"FRONT" IS THE FAMILY'S OWN FACING DIRECTION, AND IT IS WORTH CHECKING ONCE.** The zone is built on the instance's transform, so it rotates with the unit. If a family was authored facing the wrong way its front zone points into the wall and the check is confidently wrong, which is why every unit's facing direction is REPORTED rather than assumed correct. **THE EQUIPMENT'S OWN SERVICES ARE NOT OBSTRUCTIONS.** The duct plugged into the unit necessarily fills the space at its connector. Anything connected to it, and its own sub-components, are excluded - otherwise every unit reports its own pipework as blocking it and the check gets switched off. **WITHOUT `includeLinks` LINKED MODELS ARE NOT SCANNED, AND A CLEAN RESULT MAY THEREFORE HAVE CHECKED NOTHING.** Structure and architecture usually arrive as links and are exactly what blocks access. The count of host-model candidates is reported for that reason. **EVERY FIGURE IS A PER-REQUEST INPUT (D-33).** Manufacturers' clearances differ per unit; there is no default here, because a number nobody chose applied to a plant room is the failure this rule exists for. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, each unit's access zone is carried into every placement of every loaded link and tested with the same solid test; rooms, spaces and areas are not obstructions. Every unit something in a link blocks gets a line in `linkedMatches` naming the linked walls, columns or beams with their type, id IN THE LINK and **Fire Rating** - structure and architecture are exactly what blocks access, and they are usually links. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `blocked` stays this model's answer (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-family-standards"></a>

### Check family standards

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** audit the family library against the office standard and its OmniClass, Assembly Code and Keynote classification, or check the mep family open in the family editor joins its run and follows its pipe size.

Audits the families a project is using - are they named to the convention, do they carry the parameters the job needs, and do the MEP ones have connectors at all. The library check before a family set goes onto a job, and the explanation for *"why does nothing schedule properly"*. Read-only. **BEFORE THIS, ASKING WHETHER THE FAMILIES FOLLOW THE STANDARD RESOLVED TO `RENAME_FAMILY`** - a write, to a question about the model. That is the worst shape of mis-route in this library and it is the same one `REPORT_VIEW_FILTERS` was built to close. **IT AUDITS TYPES, NOT INSTANCES, AND THAT IS THE POINT.** One badly built family type placed two hundred times is ONE thing to fix. An instance-based report shows it as two hundred findings and buries everything else. Every row is a type; the instance count beside it is what makes it urgent. **NO CONNECTOR IS THE HEADLINE FINDING FOR MEP.** A terminal, a valve or a piece of equipment with no connector cannot join a system, cannot carry flow, and never appears in a system browser - but it looks perfectly normal in a plan and clashes like anything else. It is the most common reason a model looks finished and behaves as though nothing is connected. **CONNECTORS ARE READ THROUGH A PLACED INSTANCE, BECAUSE A TYPE DOES NOT EXPOSE THEM.** So a type with no instance placed cannot be checked this way and is reported as NOT CHECKED rather than as passing. That distinction is the difference between an audit and a guess. **SYSTEM FAMILIES HAVE NO FAMILY FILE** - duct types, wall types, pipe types. They are counted and excluded, never silently skipped. **THE NAMING PATTERN AND THE REQUIRED PARAMETERS ARE INPUTS (D-33).** There is no universal family standard, and a default here would be one office's convention applied to another's model. **VERSION 2 (2026-10-04, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-313): A FAMILY OPEN IN THE FAMILY EDITOR IS CHECKED ITSELF, BEFORE IT IS LOADED.** Three PPR valves built through Heron in Revit 2024 looked finished and were not: two check valves would not connect to a pipe (Work Plane-Based Yes; one also Part Type Normal), and the gate valve would not resize with its pipe (its connector's Nominal Diameter, and 35 formulas off it, were TYPE parameters). Nothing said so until each was loaded and tried. Now, in a family document, this answers PASS, FAIL or WARN for each check, with the fix in Revit words and the Heron tool that makes it where there is one, as ONE string - `familyReport` - because a list reaches the reply cut to three: - placement: an inline accessory or a fitting that is Work Plane-Based; an inline accessory whose Part Type is Normal with a run's connectors; a fitting whose Part Type is Normal; - connectors: none at all on an MEP family; one pointing toward the family's own centre (5b-309); a pass-through pair not opposite on one line; a size no family parameter drives; a size driven by a TYPE parameter, with how many formulas depend on it, or by one with a formula of its own; an inline accessory's System Classification not Global (a WARN - some offices fix it); - tidiness: a family parameter nothing uses (a FAIL; a SHARED one is a WARN, since shared ones carry schedule data); a solid form shown at Coarse or Medium inside a nested family that already draws that level (a WARN).

The checks go by CATEGORY and PART TYPE, never by the family's name: pipe and duct accessories are inline, pipe, duct, cable tray and conduit fittings are the run's joints, and equipment, terminals, fixtures and devices sit at a run's end (no Work Plane-Based or Part Type check; a size driven by a type parameter is right for them). Every other category gets the name, required parameter and tidiness checks only. `namePattern` is matched against the family's own name and `requiredParameters` against its family parameters. In a family document the version 1 audit of NESTED family types is not run: a nested handwheel needs no connector, and reporting one would be false work. Version 1's proof no longer describes the code and is kept below as a record; the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again (NEEDS-CHECKING Group CB). **VERSION 3 (2026-10-11): CLASSIFICATION, IN BOTH DOCUMENTS.** The OmniClass Number against the classification file - not in it, or filed under another category or none, is wrong; blank is a WARN in a family and only counted in a project unless `requiredParameters` names it - and each type's Assembly Code and Keynote against the document's tables, a missing table NOT CHECKED. A project's counts come back on one line, `classificationReport`. **VERSION 4 (2026-10-28, row 5b-1346): A DUCT OR PIPE FITTING'S OWN RULES.** In a Pipe Fittings or Duct Fittings family open in the Family Editor, four more checks: its run connectors counted against its Part Type - an elbow two, a tee three, a cross four, a cap one, a FAIL when they differ, and NOT CHECKED for a part whose count Heron has not recorded; each one's System Classification Fitting (a WARN); one primary, lying on the X axis (a WARN); and an elbow's connector Angle driven by an INSTANCE family parameter - by a TYPE one a FAIL, by none a WARN until Revit's own elbow is read (NEEDS-CHECKING Group JN). Version 3's proof no longer describes the code and is kept below as a record; DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-minimum-clearance"></a>

### Check minimum clearance

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** every pair of things closer together than they are allowed to be.

Measures the real gap between two sets of elements and reports **every pair** closer than the clearance required - not the nearest one, all of them. **IT IS NOT `FIND_NEAREST_ELEMENTS` WITH A THRESHOLD.** That answers *"which one is closest to each"* and returns one per element. This answers *"what is too close"* and returns every offending pair, because a duct with four services inside its clearance zone has four problems and a report naming one of them closes none of them. **INSULATION IS OPTIONAL AND IT CHANGES THE ANSWER ON EVERY REAL MEP JOB.** A 50 mm jacket on both services eats 100 mm of the gap, so a pair reading 120 mm clear on the bare geometry has 20 mm in reality and cannot be built. The earlier library kept this as a **second fragment**; here it is a flag, because it is the same sweep with each element's box grown by its own insulation, and two fragments that differ by one measurement drift apart the moment one is fixed. **A DIFFERENT CLEARANCE PER CATEGORY IS THE NORMAL CASE**, not the advanced one - 50 mm to structure, 150 mm to electrical, 300 mm to a flue is one rule set, not three runs. `rules` carries it; `defaultClearance` catches whatever the table does not name, and every pair reports which rule judged it so a wrong threshold is visible rather than buried. **THE GAP IS MEASURED BETWEEN BOUNDING BOXES AND IS THEREFORE OPTIMISTIC ON A ROTATED ELEMENT** - the box is bigger than the element, so two of them read closer than they are. That direction is the safe one for a clearance check: it over-reports rather than missing a clash. It still must not be quoted as a certified figure. **IT REPORTS AND CHANGES NOTHING.** Deciding what to move is a person's job, and a clearance sweep that also moved things would make the report unreadable by changing what it was reporting on. **MILLIMETRES IN AND MILLIMETRES OUT.** `defaultClearance` and every number in `rules` are millimetres (D-71); the gap comes back in millimetres too. Both halves were wrong and in opposite directions. `rules` was used **raw against a measurement in feet**, so `Walls=150` demanded 150 FEET and condemned every pair a rule judged while the default-judged pairs stayed right - and the rule column beside them read as the explanation rather than the fault. `gaps` then came back in feet, so the one fragment answered in two units at once. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every element is also measured against the linked walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, columns, beams, foundations and stairs near it - the same box gap, in this model's space, judged by the same rules against the linked element's category name - and each pair too close is a line in `linkedMatches` with the gap, the clearance asked for and the linked element's type, id IN THE LINK and Fire Rating. Only the element's own insulation comes off a linked gap. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `tooClose`, `gapsMm`, `judgedBy` and `pairsChecked` stay this model's own (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. **NO INSULATION MODELLED IS SAID FIRST (version 3).** With insulation counted, the insulated and bare elements are counted and a warning leads when some carry none; `assumeThicknessMm` lags them on paper, said on every row. Each pair is measured once. Version 3 is DRAFT until proved.

<a id="check-model-standards"></a>

### Check model standards

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** does this model follow the project's own naming and data rules, before it is issued.

Checks the model against the project's own naming and data conventions - view names, sheet numbers, level names, workset names, MEP system names, and whether the parameters the project requires are actually filled in. The sweep before a model is issued, and the one that finds the twelve views somebody called *"Copy of Copy of Level 1"*. It changes nothing. **THE RULES ARE PATTERNS YOU SUPPLY, NOT A STANDARD THIS FRAGMENT KNOWS.** Naming conventions are project-specific and change between employers and between clients; a fragment with one hard-coded would be wrong on every job but one. Each rule is plain text with `*` as a wildcard, which is the form somebody who owns the standard can write and check without being a programmer. **WILDCARDS ONLY, AND THAT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A LIMITATION.** The pattern language is `*` and literal text, case-insensitive. A regular expression would be more powerful and would move authorship of the standard from the person who owns it to whoever is holding the keyboard. **IT REPORTS WHAT IT COULD NOT CHECK, AND THAT IS AS IMPORTANT AS WHAT FAILED.** A rule set naming no pattern for sheets does not mean the sheets are fine - it means nobody looked. Every section says NOT CHECKED, with the reason, instead of printing a reassuring zero. This is the same defect as a filter that matches nothing and reports success, and it is the one this whole project exists around. **BLANK AND ABSENT ARE SEPARATED, BECAUSE THEY GO TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE.** A parameter that exists and is empty is data entry. A parameter that is not on the category at all is a project setup job. One combined *"empty"* number sends the work to the wrong person, and `DESCRIBE_BLANK_PARAMETERS` makes the same separation for one parameter as an actionable set. **VIEW TEMPLATES AND REVIT'S OWN INTERNAL VIEWS ARE EXCLUDED BY DEFAULT.** A project's templates rarely follow the sheet naming convention, and the browser and system views are not named by anybody. Flagging them buries the real findings under noise nobody can act on. **VERSION 2 READS FOUR MORE RULES, EVERY ONE OPTIONAL AND EVERY ONE NOT CHECKED WHEN IT IS NOT GIVEN.** They are keys in the same `namePatterns` table, not new values to supply, so a request written for version 1 runs unchanged: `type=` checks type names written as *"Family: Type"* - no space before the colon - over the types of the categories in `requiredOn`, so `type=*: TRG*` finds every type whose name does not start with the office prefix; `room=` checks room names; `value:<parameter>=` is the pattern a FILLED value of a required parameter must match, and a filled value that breaks it is counted apart from a blank one, because correcting data and entering it are different jobs; `placeholder=TBD, XXX` names the values this project uses for "not filled in yet", which are then counted as BLANK. **No placeholder is assumed** - with none named, *"TBD"* is a filled value, and the report says placeholders were NOT CHECKED. Keys are read regardless of capitals, and a key it does not know is listed as NOT USED rather than dropped. **A PARAMETER NAME TWO PARAMETERS SHARE ON ONE ELEMENT IS REPORTED, NOT READ** (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 5b-203). Revit picks one of the two at random when asked by name, so such an element is counted as NOT READ - neither passed nor failed. **A CHECK THAT PASSES MEANS THE MODEL MEETS THE RULES THAT WERE GIVEN.** It never says the model complies with anything; that is the engineer's call. **THIS CHECKS CONVENTIONS, NOT CORRECTNESS.** A view named perfectly can still show the wrong thing. It is the cheap half of a model audit; the warnings, the links and the geometry weight are the other half, and neither replaces looking at the drawings.

<a id="check-panel-flatness"></a>

### Check panel flatness

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** how far out of plane is each facade panel - is every panel flat enough for one sheet of glass.

MEASURES HOW FAR EACH PANEL'S CORNERS ARE FROM ONE FLAT PLANE - the twist a sheet of glass or a flat cladding panel would have to take on a twisted or doubly curved facade. Read-only. "Are these facade panels flat enough for glass", "how far out of plane is each panel", "check the flatness of the panels on this twisted surface". **ADAPTIVE PANELS, BY THEIR PLACEMENT POINTS.** For each adaptive component handed in - a panel placed on the nodes of a divided surface or between points - its placement points are read, the plane that fits them best is found, and its value is the furthest any corner sits from that plane, in millimetres. Every panel is listed worst first. **A PANEL HERON CANNOT READ IS NAMED, NEVER GIVEN A NUMBER.** One whose corners are not adaptive points - a curtain panel in a curtain wall, flat by construction, or a pattern-based panel whose corners the API does not return as points (an ASSUMPTION the proof settles) - and one with three points or fewer, which always lie on one plane, go in `notMeasured` with why. **THE LIMIT IS THE MODELLER'S.** `toleranceMm` left out: no panel is called flat enough or not - how much twist a sheet takes is the glazier's and the architect's number, not Heron's. Given one, the panels over it are in `overTolerance`, ready to select. Never writes anything.

<a id="check-room-mep-completeness"></a>

### Check room MEP completeness

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which rooms are missing the mep they should have.

Checks each room against a rule of what it should contain - a diffuser and an extract in every toilet, a sprinkler in every enclosed space, a detector per room - and reports per room what is missing. Read-only. **The rules are the input and there is no sensible default set.** What a room needs depends on the project, the discipline and the authority. A toilet needs extract in every specification; a store room needs it in some. So the rules come from the request and this fragment supplies none. **A device is IN a room by Revit's own boundary test, not by a bounding box.** An L-shaped room does not claim a device standing in the notch outside it - which a box would, and that is the whole reason a purpose-built test is used. **A device is placed by its insertion point, so one in the ceiling void above the room still counts.** That is what anybody wants for a diffuser and it is said out loud rather than left to be discovered. **Rooms with no area are excluded and counted, never failed.** An unplaced or unenclosed room has no boundary, so every test against it comes back false and it would report as missing everything - dozens of false failures burying the real ones. That is a different defect and it is reported as a count. **A room matching no rule is counted and listed, not passed.** Rules match on the room's NAME, so "WC 1" and "Toilet 3" need rules that catch both. A naming mismatch must never read as a clean result. **Devices in LINKED models are not counted.** If the sprinklers live in a separate fire model this reports every room as missing them, so the total found per category is printed first - a category with zero found anywhere is a link problem, not a modelling one. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link's rooms are checked with the same rules against the same devices - each device's insertion point carried into each placement's own coordinates and put to Revit's own boundary test in the link - and `linkedMatches` gives each link's count, then each short linked room with what it is short of. An MEP model places devices under the architect's rooms, so this is the answer a host-only run cannot give. Unenclosed linked rooms and linked rooms matching no rule are counted per link. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `shortRooms`, `unbounded` and `noRule` stay this model's own (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

This is the SECOND set, so `selected` is refused: the first set is what is selected<br>**rule room names** - a list - comma separated<br>**rule categories** - a list - comma separated<br>**rule minimums** - whole numbers - comma separated<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |

<a id="check-sleeve-size"></a>

### Check sleeve size

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-22 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** are the sleeves the right size for what passes through them.

Checks every sleeve against the service that actually passes through it - is the hole big enough for the pipe plus its insulation plus the annular gap the specification asks for, and is it not so oversized that fire-stopping becomes the problem instead. Read-only. **IT CHECKS SLEEVES THAT ALREADY EXIST. IT PLACES NOTHING AND CUTS NOTHING.** *"Put the sleeves in"* and *"cut the holes for the ducts"* are a different job with nothing yet in the model for this to read. **THE SERVICE IS FOUND BY GEOMETRY, NOT BY A PARAMETER.** A sleeve family almost never records what goes through it - that link is stored nowhere. So the pairing is made by asking which service actually occupies the same space. **A SLEEVE WITH NOTHING THROUGH IT IS A FINDING, NOT A BLANK ROW.** It is either an orphan left behind when a run moved, or the run moved and the hole did not. Both are real and both look like "no data" in a report that omits them. **THE REQUIRED SIZE IS ARITHMETIC AND EVERY TERM IS EXPLICIT**: the service's outside size, plus twice its insulation, plus twice the annular clearance - which is a per-request number and never a default (D-33). Insulation is read from the real insulation element rather than assumed, because a 50 mm jacket turns a comfortable sleeve into a tight one. **OVERSIZE IS REPORTED AS WELL AS UNDERSIZE**, and that is not fussiness. A hole far bigger than the service costs fire-stopping, weakens what it is cut through, and gets queried on site. **SLEEVE SIZE IS READ BY PARAMETER NAME AND FAMILIES DO NOT AGREE ON NAMES.** A list of the usual ones is tried and the one that answered is REPORTED per row, so a sleeve whose family calls it something else shows up as unreadable rather than as passing. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, each sleeve's centre is looked for inside the walls, floors, roofs, ceilings and structural members of every loaded link, in each placement's own coordinates, and `linkedMatches` names what it passes through - the link, the type, the element's id IN THE LINK and its **Fire Rating**. That is the other half of this check: an oversized sleeve through a 2-hour wall is a fire-stopping problem, and the wall is usually the architect's. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". "Passes through" is a box test, so a sleeve near a corner can name both walls - every candidate is listed. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `undersized` and `orphaned` stay this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-surface-fit"></a>

### Check surface fit

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** can this element actually sit flat against what is behind it.

For each element, fires rays from its whole FOOTPRINT rather than from its centre alone, and reports whether it can actually sit flat against what it finds. Read-only. **A SINGLE CENTRE RAY IS RIGHT IN THE MIDDLE OF A LARGE FLAT SURFACE AND LIES AT THE EDGES - AND EDGES ARE WHERE THE MISTAKES ARE.** This is the same intersection arithmetic with more sample points, and it names the four ways one ray gets it wrong: | Verdict | What it means | |---|---| | `STRADDLING` | corners hit DIFFERENT elements - it spans a ceiling edge or a level change | | `OVERHANGING` | some corners hit nothing - it hangs off the edge | | `UNEVEN` | corners hit the same element at different heights | | `SLOPED` | the surface is not square to the ray, so nothing can sit flush | **IT IS THE CHECK BEFORE `MOVE_TO_RAY_HIT`, not a replacement for it.** Its real use is deciding which elements are safe to move automatically and which need somebody to look. A batch move that includes a straddling unit puts it in the wrong place confidently. **BEFORE THIS, THE QUESTION RESOLVED TO `SNAP_TO_GRID` - which MOVES things.** A question about whether the model is right, answered by something that changes it. **IT REPORTS BY EXCEPTION.** Ray count is not the cost here; output is. A clean run over five thousand elements should print a summary line and nothing else. **LINKED MODELS ARE NOT HIT UNLESS ASKED FOR.** If the ceilings and slabs are a link, every element reports as finding nothing - which looks exactly like a real finding. Said on the summary line. **LINKED MODELS ARE HIT ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, the same five rays are cast again with Revit's own FindReferencesInRevitLinks, and every element whose rays land on a LINKED surface gets its own verdict in `linkedMatches` - the same four names, with the linked ceiling or slab's type, id IN THE LINK and Fire Rating. On an MEP model the ceilings and slabs are the architect's and the structural engineer's, so this is the check a host-only run cannot make. **The ray sees a link only where the 3D view shows it**, and the answer names that view. `linksSearched` says how many links are loaded: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `unsafeToMove` and `clean` stay this model's answer; `unsafeToMove` feeds the move (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-valve-accessibility"></a>

### Check valve accessibility

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** can these valves and dampers actually be reached and operated.

Checks that valves, dampers and other in-line accessories can actually be reached and turned - room round the handle, an access panel where one is needed, and within reach from the floor. The commissioning question, asked while it is still cheap to move things. Read-only. **IT ASKS THREE QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS EACH SEPARATELY, BECAUSE EACH HAS A DIFFERENT FIX.** *Room* - something modelled inside the operating envelope, fixed by moving the obstruction. *Above a ceiling* - fixed with an access panel, which is a drawing item and the thing most often forgotten. *Height* - fixed with a platform, a chain wheel, or relocating. A valve can pass one and fail another, so all three are reported per valve rather than one pass or fail that hides which problem it is. **ABOVE A CEILING IS NOT A FAULT, AND THIS DOES NOT PRETEND IT IS.** Most valves live in the ceiling void. The finding is that each one NEEDS AN ACCESS PANEL, and the list is what goes to the architect. A check that cries wolf about every valve in the building gets switched off by lunchtime. **THIS IS NOT CHECK_EQUIPMENT_CLEARANCE WITH SMALLER NUMBERS.** That builds a directional zone from a family's facing direction, which is right for plant and meaningless for a valve in a pipe. This asks the two questions plant does not have - is there a ceiling over it, and can a person reach it. **THE OPERATING ENVELOPE IS A PLAIN BOX, AND THAT IS STATED RATHER THAN DRESSED UP.** It is not a swept volume of a hand and a lever. It is an indication, and the figure should be the space a fitter actually needs - roughly the lever length plus a fist. **CEILINGS AND STRUCTURE IN LINKS ARE NOT SEEN UNLESS ASKED FOR.** If the architecture is linked, the ceiling question returns nothing and the room question misses the walls. That is reported on the summary line, because it looks exactly like a clean result. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, the ROOM and CEILING questions are asked of every loaded link too - the operating envelope carried into each placement and tested against the link's elements (rooms, spaces and areas are not obstructions), and the upward ray cast again with Revit's own FindReferencesInRevitLinks - and each accessory the links answer for gets a line in `linkedMatches` naming the linked obstruction or ceiling with its type, id IN THE LINK and Fire Rating. That is the access-panel list the architect actually needs, since the ceilings are theirs. **The ray sees a link only where the 3D view shows it.** `linksSearched` says how many links are loaded: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `obstructed`, `needAccessPanel` and `outOfReach` stay this model's answer (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="check-vertical-clearance"></a>

### Check vertical clearance

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how much clear vertical room is there between stacked services.

For every pair of services that sit above one another, how much clear VERTICAL space is between the bottom of the upper one and the top of the lower one, and which pairs are tighter than the rule. The *"keep 150 mm between the duct and the sprinkler main so the hangers and the insulation fit"* check - and the one that decides whether a ceiling void actually works. Read-only. **IT IS NOT CHECK_MINIMUM_CLEARANCE WITH A SMALLER NUMBER, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT.** A straight-line gap does not answer the coordination question. Two services 200 mm apart diagonally have 200 mm of straight-line clearance and may have only 40 mm of VERTICAL room - which is what a flange, a hanger and an insulation jacket actually need. This measures the Z gap only. **AND ONLY FOR PAIRS ACTUALLY ABOVE ONE ANOTHER.** Services passing at different plan positions are not a stacking problem and are correctly silent here. A report that lists them buries the real ones. **IT SAYS WHICH ONE IS ON TOP, because that is half the answer.** *"A is above B by 90 mm"* makes a service in the wrong order - drainage above the duct it has to cross under - visible as a fact rather than inferred from two elevations. **A NEGATIVE GAP IS AN OVERLAP, NOT A SMALL GAP**, and is flagged as a clash so it can never be read as *"just tight"*. **MEASURED ON BOUNDING BOXES, WHICH IS RIGHT FOR A HORIZONTAL RUN AND PESSIMISTIC FOR A SLOPED ONE.** A box hugs a level duct. For a sloped or vertical run the box is the whole rise, so the gap reported is smaller than the truth - it over-reports, never misses. Those runs are counted separately so that is visible rather than silently wrong.

<a id="compare-elements"></a>

### Compare elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-14 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what is actually different between these two elements.

Given two or more elements, reports only the parameters whose values DIFFER between them, and which value each one holds. The answer to "why is this duct behaving differently from that one" - a question that a full parameter dump cannot answer, because the difference is three rows hidden among fifty identical ones. **THE SUPPRESSION IS THE FEATURE.** A real element carries fifty to eighty parameters and on two elements of the same type nearly all of them match. Printing all of them and leaving a person to spot the difference is the same work they came here to avoid. `differing` holds only what actually differs; `identicalCount` says how many were checked and matched, so "they are the same" is a stated finding rather than an empty result that might be a failure. **VALUES ARE COMPARED AS REVIT DISPLAYS THEM, NOT AS DOUBLES.** Two ducts both drawn at 2500 mm can hold internal feet that differ in the twelfth decimal place. Compared as numbers they differ; compared as the text Revit shows, they match - and matching is the true answer, because nothing in the model behaves differently because of that noise. The cost is that a real difference smaller than the project's display rounding is invisible here, which is stated rather than hidden. **A PARAMETER MISSING FROM ONE ELEMENT IS A DIFFERENCE, AND THE MOST USEFUL ONE.** Comparing a wall against a duct, most parameters exist on only one side. Those are reported as differences with the absent side marked, rather than skipped for not being comparable - "this one has no System Name at all" is usually the answer being looked for. **TYPE PARAMETERS ARE INCLUDED AND MARKED.** If two elements differ only in their type, every difference lives on the type, and a comparison of instance parameters alone reports them as identical - a confident wrong answer to exactly the question asked.

<a id="compare-models"></a>

### Compare models

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what changed between this model and the last issue of it.

Compares the open model against another `.rvt` on disk - what was added, what was removed, and which of the named parameters changed on the elements present in both. The *"what did they change in this revision"* question answered from the two models rather than from a transmittal note. It opens the other file read-only, detached, and closes it again; neither model is modified. **`COMPARE_ELEMENTS` COMPARES TWO ELEMENTS INSIDE ONE MODEL AND THIS COMPARES TWO MODELS.** They read as the same job and are not: one answers *"why does this duct behave differently from that one"*, this one answers *"what came back different in the architect's new issue"*. Nothing in this library could ask the second question. **THE VERSION LINE IS READ BEFORE THE DIFF, AND IT IS THE PART THAT SAYS WHETHER TO BELIEVE THE REST.** Two files with the same version GUID and save count are literally the same model at the same save. Any difference reported after that is a fault in the comparison, not a change in the model - so it is checked first and stated first, rather than left for somebody to wonder about at the bottom of a long list. **ELEMENTS ARE MATCHED ON `ElementId`, AND THE SECOND MATCHING MODE WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CARRIED OVER.** The earlier library offered a composite key - category, family, type and Mark, falling back to location - for models whose ids "share no lineage", and its own note recorded that the key mode is strictly worse for the case this exists for: a save-as preserves ids, so on a model and an earlier save of itself the id IS the identity, while the composite key invents an *added* and a *removed* every time somebody edits a Mark or nudges an element. **That is precisely the noise a change report must not produce**, and offering it as an option asks the reader to choose between a right answer and a wrong one. Two genuinely unrelated models are a different question and do not have this answer. **THE FILE IS OPENED DETACHED, WITH THE WORKSETS CLOSED, AND AS THE WRONG USER.** Every real project file is workshared. A bare open touches the central; loading every workset costs minutes this comparison does not need; and the path handed over is usually somebody else's local, which Revit refuses outright without being told to allow it. All three are set unconditionally because on a non-workshared file each is harmless. **REVIT CALLS A FILE FROM ANOTHER RELEASE "CORRUPT", AND THAT WORD SENDS PEOPLE LOOKING FOR DAMAGE THAT IS NOT THERE.** The header can be read without opening the file, so when the open fails this reports which release it was saved in against which release is running, and only says damaged when those match. **A CLEAN DIFF IS NOT A PROOF THAT NOTHING CHANGED, AND THE READ-BACK SAYS SO.** Only the categories handed in are looked at and only the parameters named. A wall that changed thickness without moving reads as unchanged unless thickness is in the list. The summary states what was actually covered, so the claim stays the size of the check.

<a id="find-clashes"></a>

### Find clashes

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which of these actually intersect those.

Element-against-element clash: which members of one set physically intersect members of another. Ducts against beams, pipes against structure, services against each other. **This is NOT `PROBE_AROUND_ELEMENTS`, and the two get asked for in the same words.** That one casts a ray from a POINT and asks what is within a distance of it — the sprinkler-under-a-beam question, answered before anything is modelled. This one takes two sets of REAL ELEMENTS and asks whose solids overlap. A layout check and a coordination check. **Solids, not bounding boxes.** A bounding box says a diagonal duct clashes with everything in the rectangle around it, which is how a clash report grows to four hundred rows nobody reads. Revit's own intersection filter tests the real geometry. **Touching is not clashing, and Revit does not draw that line for you.** A duct sitting exactly on a beam soffit reports as intersecting. That is correct geometrically and is not a defect on site, so it is reported like any other hit and the caller decides — this fragment does not invent a tolerance, because a tolerance invented here is one quietly relied on. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as version 1 did. With it set, each element's solids are carried into every placement of every loaded link and tested against that link's walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, columns, beams, foundations and stairs - the building, not another trade's MEP - and `linkedMatches` gives each link's count, then names each clashing element with the linked element's type, id IN THE LINK and **Fire Rating**, up to fifty a link. An element with no solid is counted as not tested against the links, never as clear. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `clashes`, `clashing`, `clear` and `notChecked` stay this model's own (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. **WHAT EACH ONE PASSES THROUGH, AND A PARAMETER AGAINST IT (version 3).** `passedThrough` names, element by element, everything its solid passes through - in the links, in `against`, and with `includeHost` in this model - with the category, 'Family: Type', its thickness (a wall's width, a floor's layers, anything else its depth along the element's facing or run) and which side of the element's centre it sits. `categories` says what is looked for: left out, the building list above; `all`, any model category; or names. `compareParameter` names a length on the element, and `comparison` lists every element whose value differs from the thickness it passes through - `mismatched` holds them, this model's own. An element with no solid is tested by its bounding box, and says so. Version 3, and DRAFT until proved.

<a id="find-degenerate-lines"></a>

### Find degenerate lines

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the lines that are too short to be real, that nobody can see or select.

Finds lines and other curve-driven elements that are shorter than a stated length - the accidental double-click leftovers nobody can see, select or delete by hand. **`FIND_OVERLAPPING_LINES` IS A DIFFERENT DEFECT.** That one finds lines drawn ON TOP of each other, which are each perfectly real and visible. A degenerate line is one with almost no length at all: it prints as nothing, it cannot be picked without a crossing window, and it sits in the model inflating counts and tripping up anything that walks geometry. Nothing looked for them. **THE THRESHOLD IS THE CALLER'S AND THERE IS NO SENSIBLE DEFAULT.** Revit's own short-curve tolerance is about 0.8 mm; a detail line of 2 mm is equally certainly a mistake and a 50 mm one might be deliberate. A number invented here would become a number quietly relied on, so it is asked for (D-33). **IT REPORTS AND DELETES NOTHING.** This is a READ. `DELETE_ELEMENTS` is the other half and it reports the true blast radius first, which matters: deleting a line can take a dimension with it. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

### Find duplicate elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which of these are the same thing placed twice in the same spot.

Finds elements of the same type sitting at the same place, and hands back the EXTRA ones - every member of each cluster except one. **A double-placed element is invisible and counts twice.** Two diffusers in the same spot look like one on every drawing and in every view, and appear as two in the schedule, in the count and in the quantity take-off. Nobody sees it by looking; it is found by counting, or by somebody on site. **It is a READ, and before this fragment that sentence got a WRITE.** *"Find duplicate elements"* resolved to RENAME_ELEMENTS. This one deletes nothing - it narrows `elements` to the extras so the next step can select them, isolate them, or delete them **as a separate decision somebody makes**. **Same TYPE and same PLACE, both required.** Two different diffuser types at one point is a design clash, not a duplicate, and reporting it here would put a real coordination problem in a list people bulk-delete from.

Read-only; it moves nothing and renumbers nothing. **This is duplicate DATA, and FIND_DUPLICATE_ELEMENTS is duplicate GEOMETRY.** Two elements stacked in the same place is a modelling accident. Two elements in different rooms with the same mark is a scheduling error that survives every visual check and comes out on the drawing. The two questions share the word "duplicate" and nothing else, so both fragments carry the same routing table. **A blank is not a duplicate**, and that decision is the difference between a usable report and 400 rows. On a real model most elements have no Mark at all; grouping them together would report the whole model as one enormous clash. Blanks are counted and named as a separate figure, because "180 of these have no mark" is its own finding and often the more useful one. **Values are compared as Revit renders them.** A number parameter reading "150 mm" is compared as "150 mm", because that is what a schedule prints and what somebody reads on a drawing. Comparing the raw internal double would report two elements as different over a rounding difference nobody can see.

<a id="find-overlapping-lines"></a>

### Find overlapping lines

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-17 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** find the lines drawn on top of each other.

Finds lines drawn on top of each other - exact duplicates and partly overlapping collinear segments. The cleanup for a view that prints heavy for no visible reason, and for imported CAD exploded into hundreds of stacked lines. Read-only: it reports, and deletes nothing. **"Are these two lines the same" is not a comparison you can do directly**, and that is the whole content of this fragment. Two lines that look identical almost never have equal endpoints: they were drawn in opposite directions, they overlap only partly, or floating point puts them a millionth of a foot apart. Comparing endpoints finds nearly nothing. What works is to give each line the identity of the INFINITE LINE IT SITS ON and group by that - direction, then perpendicular distance from the origin. Three things make that work and each one is a defect if skipped: 1. **Normalise the direction.** Drawn left-to-right and right-to-left give opposite vectors. Flip every direction into one half-plane first, or the two never match - the commonest reason an overlap check "finds nothing". 2. **Round both the direction and the offset before they become the key.** Unrounded floats put genuinely collinear lines in different groups. 3. **Only then compare along the line.** Within a group everything is collinear, so each line is a one-dimensional interval and overlapping is interval arithmetic.

**Line style is part of the identity.** Two lines on one alignment in different styles are usually deliberate - a grid line and a hidden line - and calling them duplicates would have somebody delete a drawing convention. **Only straight lines.** Arcs and splines are counted and reported as skipped; collinearity has no meaning for them and pretending otherwise would put real geometry on a delete list.

<a id="propose-mep-openings"></a>

### Propose MEP openings

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** where the services go through, and how big the hole needs to be.

Finds where MEP runs pass through walls and floors, and PROPOSES an opening at each one - position, size and the host it belongs to. **It creates nothing.** **PROPOSING AND CREATING ARE DELIBERATELY TWO OPERATIONS.** Cutting holes in somebody's structure is not a thing to do as a side effect of looking for them. The list this produces is meant to be read, argued with, and only then acted on - by a separate write that somebody approved. That split is the plan's own recommendation and it is the right way round: an audit that quietly modifies is not an audit. **AUDIT_MEP_OPENINGS AND CHECK_SLEEVE_SIZE INSPECT WHAT EXISTS. THIS PROPOSES WHAT DOES NOT.** They answer *"are the openings there right"*; this answers *"where do openings need to be"*. On a model with no openings drawn yet, they have nothing to report and this has everything. **THE ALLOWANCE IS REQUIRED, NOT ASSUMED.** How much bigger than the duct a hole must be is a project decision - it varies by trade, by fire rating and by who is paying for the sleeve. Assuming a number would produce a schedule of holes that look authoritative and match nobody's specification. **IT MEASURES THE REAL INTERSECTION, NOT A BOUNDING BOX.** A duct crossing a wall at an angle needs a bigger hole than its own width, and a bounding-box answer would be right only for a perpendicular crossing. The solid is intersected with the run's centre line, so an oblique penetration reports the length it really cuts. **A RUN THROUGH TWO WALLS IS TWO OPENINGS.** Each intersected segment is reported separately, with its own host, because that is how many holes have to be cut. Reads only. Opens no transaction and needs none. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, each service's centre line is carried into every placement of every loaded link and intersected with that link's walls, floors, roofs, ceilings and structural members - the same real intersection, never a box - and `linkedMatches` proposes every crossing: the linked host's type, its id IN THE LINK and its **Fire Rating**, the hole size, the depth through it and its centre in THIS model's coordinates. That is the owner's case: *"my pipe crosses a linked wall and I need to create something there - is it a 2-hour wall?"* With links read, an empty `hosts` is not refused, because the hosts are expected to be in the links. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `proposals`, `hostIds` and `runIds` stay this model's own; `hostIds` feeds the step that cuts, and a hole in a linked wall is cut in that model by whoever owns it (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Answers a question (`READ`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **hosts** - a CATEGORY name - "Ducts", or "Ducts, Duct Fittings" for more than one - and it means every one in the MODEL, not in a view. This is the SECOND set, so `selected` is refused: the first set is what is selected<br>**allowance mm** - a number - digits only - 250 or 250.5, not 250mm<br>**include links** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | proposals, host ids, run ids, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |

<a id="read-model-warnings"></a>

### Read model warnings

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** what warnings is this model carrying, and which elements cause them.

Reads the model's warning list, groups it by what the warning actually says, and hands on the elements causing them. **The elements are the point, not the count.** *"How many warnings"* got answered by COUNT_ELEMENTS before this existed - a number about something else entirely. But a warning count on its own is a number nobody can act on; what a modeller needs next is to SEE the elements, and because this fragment provides `elements`, *"show me what is causing the warnings"* composes straight into ISOLATE_ELEMENTS or SET_SELECTION. **Grouped by message, because that is how warnings actually arrive.** A model with 800 warnings usually has six kinds of problem, and one of them is 600 rows of the same duplicate-instance message. A flat list of 800 is unreadable and hides the five that matter. **ERRORS ONLY, OR ONE KIND OF WARNING (version 2).** `errorsOnly` keeps the Error severity; `descriptionContains` the warnings whose text holds a phrase. An empty answer is not a clean model.

|---|---|
| **Kind** | Answers a question (`READ`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **errors only** - yes or no - true or false; optional<br>**description contains** - text; optional, left out means *none* |
| **You get** | elements, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `READ_MODEL_WARNINGS` |

<a id="report-constraints"></a>

### Report constraints

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** what is holding this element, and what moves with it.

What is locking each element in place - the locked dimensions and alignments holding it - and what is on the other end of each one. **A CONSTRAINT IS INVISIBLE UNTIL YOU GO LOOKING, AND THAT IS AN API FACT RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT.** It is not a property *of* the element. It is a separate element that holds references to two or more things. There is no `wall.Constraints` to read, so the only way to find what is holding something is to walk **every** constraint in the model and check whether any of its references points back. That is why this is slow, and why nothing surfaces it by accident. **IT ANSWERS "WHY WILL THIS NOT MOVE", WHICH `REPORT_ELEMENT_DEPENDENCIES` DOES NOT.** That one answers *"what goes with it if I delete it"*. An element can have no dependents at all and still be locked to three others - and moving it then moves them, or refuses. The two are neighbours and neither covers the other: | The question | Use | |---|---| | "what disappears if I delete this" | `REPORT_ELEMENT_DEPENDENCIES` | | "why will this not move", "what moves with it" | **this fragment** | **THE FAR END IS THE USEFUL HALF.** Knowing an element is constrained tells nobody anything. Knowing it is locked to *that column* is the whole answer, so every other element on each constraint is reported. **IT REPORTS AND NEVER UNLOCKS.** Removing a constraint is not cosmetic: deleting a locked dimension deletes the **dimension**, so the annotation disappears from the drawing along with the lock - which is almost never what anybody means by *"unlock it"*. That decision needs a person, and a read fragment must not make it.

| **You get** | constrained by, locked to |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |
| **Capability** | `REPORT_CONSTRAINTS` |

<a id="report-element-dependencies"></a>

### Report element dependencies

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what else goes if this element goes.

For each element, what Revit would take away with it - the tags, dimensions, hosted families, sketch lines and openings - and, separately, whether Revit would allow the deletion at all. Asked BEFORE the change rather than discovered after it. **THE LIST IS REVIT'S OWN, NOT ONE ASSEMBLED HERE.** `GetDependentElements(null)` returns what Revit itself considers attached - the same set it removes on delete. It reaches things nothing could reasonably derive: a tag that references the element, a dimension witnessed on it, a family hosted in it, the sketch a floor is drawn from, an opening cut through it. **THE LIST ALWAYS CONTAINS THE ELEMENT ITSELF.** That is not a defect and it must not be stripped blindly - it is why a count reads one higher than expected. It is excluded from `dependents` and reported as its own fact, so the number is never quietly wrong in either direction. **"CAN I DELETE IT" IS A SECOND QUESTION AND REVIT ANSWERS IT DIRECTLY.** An element can have zero dependents and still be undeletable - pinned, the last level, owned by another user in a workshared model. Both are asked, because either one alone gives a confident wrong answer to "is this safe to remove". **JOINED AND CUT ARE REPORTED SEPARATELY AND ON PURPOSE.** Revit does not delete a joined neighbour; it re-cleans the geometry. A wall joined to three others changes shape when one goes, and that change appears in a drawing nobody was looking at. Folding it in with the dependents would say the wrong thing about it in both directions. **WHAT IT CANNOT SEE, SAID OUT LOUD:** a reference from a linked model, and which sheets show the element. A clean report here does not mean nothing downstream breaks.

<a id="report-element-ownership"></a>

### Report element ownership

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** whether these elements can be edited, or belong to somebody else right now.

On a workshared model, who owns each element right now, who created it and who changed it last - asked before a bulk edit rather than discovered halfway through one. **A BATCH IS ONE UNDO ENTRY, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS ASKED FIRST.** Golden Rule 16 means every fragment in a batch runs inside one transaction. Hitting an element owned by somebody else partway through does not stop at that element - it takes the whole batch with it. Knowing beforehand which elements are not editable turns that into a decision rather than a failure. **"NOT OWNED" MEANS "PROBABLY FREE", NEVER "GUARANTEED FREE", AND THIS IS STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED.** Checkout status reflects the last sync. Somebody may have borrowed an element since, and nothing local can see that. The fresh-reads rule applies to people as well as to geometry, and a report that reads as a guarantee here would be believed. **A MODEL THAT IS NOT WORKSHARED IS ANSWERED, NOT REFUSED.** `notWorkshared` says so plainly, because "everything is editable" is the correct answer to the question and an empty result would read as "nothing is editable" - the opposite of the truth, on the more common kind of model. **CREATOR, OWNER AND LAST CHANGED BY ARE THREE DIFFERENT PEOPLE** and are returned separately. Who to ask for a relinquish is the owner. Who to ask about an odd piece of modelling is the last person to change it. Collapsing them sends the question to the wrong desk. **AN ELEMENT WHOSE STATUS CANNOT BE READ IS HELD, NEVER FREE AND NEVER DROPPED** (version 2). It goes in `ownedByOthers` with owner "unknown", so the editable and held lists always add up to what was handed in. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code and is kept as a record, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="report-mirrored-instances"></a>

### Report mirrored instances

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which family instances of these categories are mirrored, and which are only flipped.

Lists the doors, fixtures, equipment - any family instances of the categories you name - that have been MIRRORED, and separately the ones whose flip arrows have been used, counted per category and per *"Family: Type"*, with every element's id. It changes nothing. **A MIRRORED DOOR SCHEDULES THE WRONG HANDING.** Mirroring reflects the geometry: a left-hand door now draws as a right-hand one while its type, its schedule row and anything ordered from that schedule still say left. Nothing in Revit warns about it, so it is found by looking, and this is the looking. **MIRRORED AND FLIPPED ARE DIFFERENT, AND ARE NEVER FOLDED TOGETHER.** A flip uses the family's own hand or facing arrows - the family author allowed it, and a flipped door is NOT a mirrored door. One instance can be mirrored AND flipped. So each of the three flags is counted on its own and printed per element, and `mirrored`, `handFlipped` and `facingFlipped` are three lists. A facing flip matters too: it leaves the door's From Room and To Room as they were (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 5b-212), and REPORT_DOOR_ROOM_LINKS is what checks those against the rooms. **FAMILY INSTANCES ONLY, AND A CATEGORY WITH NONE IS SAID.** Ducts, pipes and walls are not families and carry no such flag. A category named with no family instances in it is reported as that - never as a zero that reads like a pass. **WHAT IS NOT CHECKED:** linked models; whether a mirrored instance is actually wrong (some families are drawn to be mirrored); and a nested shared component, which turns with the family it sits in - such a row names the family it is nested in and is NOT counted in any total, so one mistake is not counted twice.

<a id="report-model-dashboard"></a>

### Report model dashboard

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the whole model at a glance - elements by category, level and workset, warnings, views and sheets, families, groups, links, CAD, rooms and spaces - in one read.

Reads the open project once and counts what it holds, part by part, for the Heron Companion's Model Dashboard: the placed model elements by category, by level and by workset, and those on no level; the warnings grouped by what they say, errors first; the views by type, which are on a sheet and which have no view template; the sheets, the empty ones and the placeholders; the loaded and in-place families and those with nothing placed; the model and detail group types and the unused ones; each Revit link file, loaded and pinned or not; the CAD files, linked or imported; and the rooms and Spaces that are not placed or have no area. Given parameter names, it also counts, per category, the elements where each one is filled in, left empty, or not there at all. Given breakdowns, it groups the elements of the categories each names for the Companion's boards, with a total where one is asked. **Counts, never a verdict.** Nothing here calls a model clean, healthy or compliant, and there is no score. A part it could not read is said, never shown as zero. **It changes nothing.** A family document is not a project: only its title is read and every part says so. **Why one string.** A fragment's list output reaches the caller as its first three names (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-195), so the dashboard crosses as one JSON string, `dashboardJson`, format 1, as REPORT_SPACE_ENVELOPE's take-off does.
